title: When to Use Redux
description: Learn the trade-offs of Redux, when it is worth adding to a project, and how modern Redux Toolkit simplifies the Redux workflow.

data.text: Redux has been one of the most debated topics in the React ecosystem. Many teams reach for it immediately; others avoid it entirely. The right answer depends on your application's complexity, your team's familiarity with the patterns, and the problems you are actually trying to solve.

Modern Redux — specifically **Redux Toolkit** — is far simpler than the Redux of the past. But even with those improvements, Redux is still a significant architectural choice that should be made deliberately.

items: A single, predictable store for your application state
Strict unidirectional data flow that is easy to debug
Powerful middleware for logging, async logic, and side effects
Predictable state updates through pure reducer functions

data.text: Redux enforces that all state changes flow through a single reducer function. This means every change is a plain object describing what happened. For complex applications with many contributors, that predictability can be invaluable.

Redux makes the most sense when you have complex state logic that needs to be shared widely, or when you need advanced debugging and state inspection across your entire application. If many unrelated components need to read and update the same data, or if you need to replay state changes during development, Redux is a strong candidate.

rows: No need for a global store
Auth status and user data across app
Auth is server state; cache it with a query library
Complex dashboard with many interacting widgets
Cart logic benefits from centralized reducer

data.text: Redux Toolkit removes the boilerplate that made classic Redux painful. You configure the store with `configureStore`, define slices with `createSlice`, and access state with `useSelector`. Async logic uses `createAsyncThunk` and `createListenerMiddleware` instead of manually wiring middleware.

data.text: Do not use Redux for server state. Use React Query for data that comes from an API. Redux is best for client-side state that many components need to coordinate. Keeping API responses in Redux means reimplementing caching, deduplication, and refetching that React Query already handles.

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Redux adds predictability and powerful debugging at the cost of boilerplate
Redux Toolkit removes most of the boilerplate from classic Redux
Prefer Redux for complex shared client state, not for server data
Use React Query for server state and Context for simple global concerns
